On New Year's Eve Yanzhi ate a whole bowl of pork stewed with glass noodles clean. It was as though she had never tasted anything so good; she sat on the bed cradling the bowl, dazed. At midnight the cell door was suddenly opened. A guard called her name from outside and told her to put on her clothes and come out. Yanzhi woke with a start from her dreaming and, thinking she was still inside a dream, pinched her thigh hard. The stabbing pain left her dumb as a wooden chicken. Yanzhi had long since heard that many prisoners were dragged out to be shot in the dead of night.
The guard urged her from outside: "Hurry up, don't dawdle."

Wrapped in a padded jacket, Yanzhi went to the door and only then found she had forgotten her shoes. She went back in to put them on and came out again, but could no longer drag her two legs along at all; she swayed and collapsed to the floor. A guard hauled Yanzhi up by one hand and all but dragged her down the long corridor; at the head of the stairs a second guard took her other side, and together they carried her down and across the pitch-black drill-ground.

In a room where a stove was burning Yanzhi met the Mrs. Qin of former days. She had a greatcoat over her shoulders and puttees wound about her legs, plainly a woman cadre of the People's Liberation Army. Yanzhi stood trembling, and it was a good while before she heard her say, "Lift your head." Yanzhi raised her head and, at a loss, narrowed her eyes.
"Do you still know me?"
Yanzhi stared at the face before her a good while, then shook her head.
"You really don't know me anymore? We met in Shanghai."
Yanzhi looked at her and shook her head again.
"Your history has been cleared up." As she spoke she picked up a file from the table and gave it a shake. "Tomorrow you can go," she added.
Yanzhi could not believe her ears. She opened her eyes wide, looked at the woman before her, and asked, "You're not going to shoot me?"
"This is the order for your release." As she spoke she put a sheet of paper into Yanzhi's hand. "Someone has vouched for your history."

For a long moment Yanzhi's eyes never went to the document, but stayed fixed hard on the face of the woman standing before her. Then all at once she said, hesitating, "I remember now. You're Mrs. Qin."
"I am the wife of Comrade Qin Shuji. My name is Yang Shuqin."
Yanzhi said, "The two of you were a false married couple."
"We were a false couple before. Now it's real." Yang Shuqin said, "We married last year."
Yanzhi nodded and said nothing.
Yang Shuqin said, "It was he who vouched for your history."
Yanzhi still said nothing, as though her two lips had been glued shut.
Yang Shuqin said, "But I know that he told a lie for you. For your sake, he deceived the organization."
Yanzhi said, "And did he not deceive me?"
Yang Shuqin said, "You can go now. Tomorrow someone will see you out."
"Yes." Yanzhi stood to attention, bowed, then walked to the door with her head down like a puppet.

Yang Shuqin said suddenly, "Wait." Yanzhi stopped and turned back, and she heard Yang Shuqin say that Qin Shuji was dead, fallen in the fighting to liberate southern Zhejiang. The last thing Qin Shuji did before he died was to certify, on the very file that examined Yanzhi's history, that she was clean. Leaning in Yang Shuqin's arms, he signed his name and had no strength left to speak; he only looked at her, as if in entreaty, and more still as if in remembrance. Yang Shuqin would never forget the look in his eyes as his breath went out. She spoke now word by word, and never noticed the greatcoat sliding from her shoulders. Yanzhi's glance fell on the black mourning-band bound about her left arm. It was that black band that made Yanzhi remember Qin Shuji's face, and the tears sprang from her eyes on the instant. But there was no grief in Yang Shuqin's eyes; her gaze was like a splinter of shattered ice, sharp and cold. She stared hard at Yanzhi, came toward her step by step, and said, word by word, "But you are the one stain of his whole life."
Yanzhi was flustered and did not know what to do. In a rush she explained, "I'm not."
Yang Shuqin said, with certainty, "You are."
